You are a professional biblical lexicographer fluent in Spanish. Translate the following English lexicon entry into Spanish.

Lemma: H7682

ENGLISH GLOSSES TO TRANSLATE:
  Terse gloss: "Be inaccessibly high; set on high for protection; be exalted in status or honor (Qal, Niphal, Piel, Hifil, Pual)"
  Readable gloss: "A verb whose core image is height that puts something beyond reach. In the Qal it describes a city wall too high to scale (Deut 2:36) or persons lifted beyond trouble (Job 5:11). The Niphal turns this into exaltation—Isaiah repeatedly applies it to the LORD alone being 'lifted high' on the coming Day (Isa 2:11, 17). In the Piel, God becomes the active protector who sets the righteous on a high crag out of danger's reach (Ps 91:14). Spanish 'poner en alto' and German 'beschützen' both capture this protective elevation that runs through the Psalms."

SENSES:
  Sense 1: "Piel: set on high, protect"
    Enriched: Piel intensive-causative: God actively places someone on an inaccessible height as refuge. Spanish 'lo pondré en alto' and English 'set on high' converge on protective elevation. Central to the Psalter's theology of divine shelter (Ps 20:1; 91:14; 107:41), where height equals safety rather than mere geography.
    Existing Spanish translations: Y-levanta, Y-levantará, lo-pondré-en-alto, me-ponga-en-alto, protégeme, te-proteja
  Sense 2: "Niphal: be exalted"
    Enriched: Niphal passive-stative of exaltation applied almost exclusively to God or his name. Isaiah's refrain 'the LORD alone shall be exalted' (2:11, 17) and the hymnic 'his name alone is exalted' (Ps 148:13) show the term reserved for divine majesty. Spanish 'ensalzado' and German 'erhöht' mirror this honorific sense.
    Existing Spanish translations: ensalzado, es-exaltado, exaltado, y-será-exaltado
  Sense 3: "Niphal: be high, lofty, inaccessible"
    Enriched: Niphal denoting physical, often forbidding height—walls about to break (Isa 30:13), a fortified city brought low (Isa 26:5), or knowledge too lofty to grasp (Ps 139:6). The multilingual evidence splits: English favors 'high/lofty' while Spanish uses 'exaltada,' showing how literal and metaphorical height blur.
    Existing Spanish translations: alto, exaltada
  Sense 4: "Qal: be inaccessibly high"
    Enriched: Qal stative: the simplest stem describes something inherently too high for human access. Deuteronomy 2:36 reports no city 'too high for us,' while Job 5:11 lifts the lowly to prosperity. With only two occurrences, this is the root's semantic base from which all derived stems elaborate.
    Existing Spanish translations: fuera-demasiado-alta, son-elevados
  Sense 5: "Niphal: be safe, secure"
    Enriched: Niphal specialized sense of security through elevation, attested once in Proverbs 18:10: the righteous runs into the name of the LORD 'and is safe.' Spanish 'es puesto en alto' underscores that safety is the outcome of being placed high, bridging Niphal stative with Piel causative protection.
    Existing Spanish translations: y-es-puesto-en-alto
  Sense 6: "Hifil: exalt, make high"
    Enriched: Hifil causative: to exalt or make high, occurring in Job 36:22 of God who 'exalts by his power.' This is the active transitive counterpart to the Niphal passive exaltation, with Spanish 'exaltado' and English 'exalts' confirming the straightforward causative reading.
    Existing Spanish translations: exaltado
  Sense 7: "Pual: be set securely on high"
    Enriched: Pual passive of the Piel: to be placed securely on high by another's agency. Proverbs 29:25 promises that whoever trusts the LORD 'will be set on high.' Spanish 'será puesto en alto' perfectly mirrors the passive construction, confirming that the agent of elevation is God himself.
    Existing Spanish translations: será-puesto-en-alto
